big: Two colleagues earn very different salaries. The lower earner has a score of 790 and the higher earner has 640. The score does not look at salary at all. It looks at behaviour.

lines: My salary is good. Why was my card application refused?
Income is not part of the score. Late payments and a maxed-out card are. Let us see what moves it.

title: Credit score habits
stops: Paying on time carries the most weight
A higher income raises your score
Using most of your card limit can lower it
Checking your own report lowers the score
caps: Payment history counts most, and a few days late is recorded.
Income is not part of the score. Behaviour is.
Keep use of your limit below about 30% to show you are not stretched.
Checking your own report is safe, and it helps you catch errors.

small: a common ceiling for card use
alt: Bars showing credit card use against a ₹1 lakh limit
caps: A card has a ₹1 lakh limit. Bars show the share used.
Using ₹10,000 is 10% of the limit, which looks comfortable.
At ₹60,000, 60%, the card looks stretched, and the score can fall.

q: Meena earns a lot but pays her card two weeks late. What happens to her score?
opts: It rises, because her income is high
It stays the same, since it ignores payments
It resets to zero for a year
It can fall, since late payment is recorded
why: Income is not part of the score, so a high one does not offset lateness.
Payments are the main input, so the score does not ignore them.
A late payment lowers the score. It does not reset it to zero.
Payment history carries the most weight, so late payment drags the score down.

q: Rohan's card limit is ₹2 lakh. Which monthly spend keeps use near 30%?
why: ₹1.5 lakh is 75% of the limit, which is high and can hurt the score.
Thirty percent of ₹2 lakh is ₹60,000, in line with the usual ceiling.
₹1.9 lakh is 95%, very close to the limit and a warning sign.
Using the full limit shows the highest strain on a card.

q: Meena checks her own credit report and finds a loan she never took. What should she do?
opts: Ignore it, since it will vanish on its own
Pay the loan to be safe
Raise a dispute with the bureau and the lender
Close all her cards at once
why: Wrong entries do not vanish by themselves, and they can hurt her score.
Paying a loan she never took would be a loss, and leaves the error on record.
Errors can be corrected, but only if she raises a dispute with them.
Closing cards does not remove a wrong loan from her report.

q: A stranger says he can 'fix your score fast' for a fee. What is the honest view?
opts: Be careful, scores improve with behaviour
Pay him, since fast fixes are common
Give him your card details to speed things up
Take a new loan to help him out
why: A score is rebuilt slowly by paying on time and keeping card use low.
Quick-fix claims for a fee are a warning sign, and nothing is gained by paying.
Sharing card details is risky and can lead to fraud.
A new loan does not fix a score, and it adds debt.

pts: Income is not in the score. Payment history and card use are.
Pay on time, and keep card use below about 30% of the limit.
Check your own report for errors. Beware of anyone selling a fast fix.
